A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SweRank and SWELOC. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched reliably across the substantial additions and reformatting.

before.justification: V1 reports original retriever and reranker experiments on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, training-data ablations, and SWELOC topic analysis.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds downstream repair, multilingual evaluation, capacity and mining studies, latency measurements, and error analyses.

M1.justification: The main architecture and both training losses are unchanged. Appendix E adds an evaluated iterative mining variant: second-round negatives are selected using the first-round trained small encoder, extending v1's described mining with pretrained CodeRankEmbed. This is a limited procedural addition, without evidence that the retained main results changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds downstream issue resolution using SWE-Fixer on SWE-Bench-Lite, extending evaluation beyond localization. Appendix F adds SWE-Bench Multilingual, covering 234 tasks across nine non-Python programming languages. The existing SWELOC training data and two main localization benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: New comparisons include Gemini-Embedding, Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B and 8B, and SWE-Fixer's native localization plus an oracle repair control. Appendix B also compares Llama reranker training variants. Conversely, both Agentless rows disappear from SWE-Bench-Lite Table 1, although Agentless remains in LocBench Table 2.

E3.justification: The existing 274-example SWE-Bench-Lite and 560-example LocBench evaluations and Appendix A training settings remain unchanged. New protocols include repair Pass@1 with an oracle control, complexity and lexical/semantic-overlap stratification, Acc@20/50/100 retrieval evaluation, controlled embedding-dimension experiments, and latency measurements over 50 instances with a matched GPT-4o comparison.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of downstream repair, issue complexity, lexical and semantic overlap, retrieval ceilings, encoder capacity and embedding dimension, iterative negative mining, latency and token use, and two qualitative localization cases. The original filtering and data-size studies remain, merged into Figure 5; the topic analysis moves from Appendix B to I.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new latency and token averages are point estimates and do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Retained numerical entries in Tables 1–5 are identical, with Agentless entries removed from Table 1. Substantial new results include repair Pass@1 of 24.5% for SweRank versus 22.6% for LocAgent (Table 6), multilingual retriever Acc@10 of 50.85% versus Gemini's 47.44% (Table 11), and matched GPT-4o latency of 30.2 versus 85.3 seconds (Table 12).

T1.justification: The contrastive loss, positive-identifier reranker objective, and associated mathematical definitions are retained. V2 numbers the existing equations but adds no theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation; the new capacity and overlap studies are empirical.

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged apart from formatting. The introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: the retrieve-and-rerank framework, SWELOC training data, state-of-the-art localization on the two main benchmarks, and favorable efficiency relative to agentic methods.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of retrieval and repair bottlenecks, failure on complex issues, semantic matching beyond lexical overlap, and transfer beyond Python. It attributes reranking gains to cross-function dependencies and discusses agents confusing symptom locations with underlying causes. These substantially extend v1's discussion of data quality, model choice, and cost.

D1.justification: V1 promises future code, data, and model releases; v2 reports code and models available through a repository. V2 also documents file/module score aggregation and latency hardware. Appendix A is unchanged, while the token-pricing footnote and agent-result provenance notes in Tables 1–2 are removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for Llama, Gemini-Embedding, Qwen3-Embedding, Matryoshka learning, SWE-Fixer, and SWE-smith. It removes the Böhme localization study, Wang's weakly supervised embeddings reference, and the Agentless reference. The related-work taxonomy and positioning of ranking against agentic localization remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Several introductory, related-work, analysis, and concluding passages are condensed or polished, and dataset and metric descriptions are combined. New result subsections and appendices are integrated, the old topic appendix is relocated, and acknowledgements are removed. The main section sequence and much existing wording remain intact.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to a single-column conference layout, substantially relocating and resizing displays. Original Figures 5 and 6 become Figure 5(a–b), Figure 3 gains a cumulative-distribution curve, and new Tables 6–13 and Figures 6–10 present added studies. The original topic plot is retained as Figure 11.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked downstream repair, explicit non-Python transfer, and measured latency validation. V2 addresses these important gaps through repair comparisons with an oracle control, multilingual evaluation, and a matched-model latency experiment (Tables 6, 11, and 12). The added failure analyses also clarify practical boundaries. These gains outweigh the lost pricing and provenance details, although some new mechanism explanations remain inferential.
